description: We are a team of high school students passionate about computer science, technology and innovation. Our combined skills span software development, multiple programming languages, hardware engineering, robotics, AI and machine learning. We enjoy building innovative solutions to real-world problems by combining software and hardware. Our team is already complete, and we are not seeking additional members.
summary: Falaj Fields is a web app and low-cost field sensor that helps UAE farmers adapt their crops to extreme heat, scarce water and salty soil. Named after the traditional falaj irrigation channels, it combines three NASA datasets: SMAP for soil moisture, NASA POWER for temperature and humidity, and ECOSTRESS for field-level heat and water stress alongside GPM. Farmers can view their land on a satellite map, get heat stress alerts, and use a rotation planner to compare their current crops with alternatives, such as legume cover crops or different crop families, against their seasonal water budget. Planting windows follow the UAE’s official calendar, and short video guides with English and Arabic captions explain cover crops and how to trial them, including between palm rows. Our solar-powered ESP32 sensor measures soil moisture in the field, with salinity and temperature sensing, to give farm-level readings that satellites alone cannot. Falaj Field turns NASA data into practical decisions that help farms save water and stay productive as the climate gets hotter.
details:
What it does

Falaj Field is a two-part project that helps UAE farmers adapt to extreme heat, scarce water and salty soil, in response to the “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data” challenge. A web app turns NASA Earth observation data into practical decisions about crop rotation, and a low-cost solar-powered sensor adds real readings from individual farms.

How it works

Our web app (pump-palm.vercel.app) combines NASA datasets, each with a specific role. SMAP shows how soil moisture changes across the UAE through the year. NASA POWER provides temperature and humidity data for our heat stress periods and seasonal planting calendar. ECOSTRESS identifies field-level heat and water stress.

Farmers can view their land on a satellite map with date-selectable NASA layers, and use a rotation planner to compare their current rotation with alternatives, such as a legume cover crop or a different crop family, against their seasonal water budget. Planting windows follow the UAE Ministry of Climate Change and Environment calendar. Short video guides, narrated in English with English and Arabic captions, explain how cover crops protect soil and how to trial them on a single strip, including between palm rows.

Our hardware is an ESP32-based field sensor that measures soil moisture, salinity and temperature. It runs on a solar panel and rechargeable battery, sends readings over Wi-Fi to the app, and sits in a 3D-printed enclosure designed for UAE heat, dust and water.

Impact

Falaj Field helps farmers identify vulnerable periods in the growing cycle, reduce water waste and improve long-term soil health, without replacing traditional farming methods. It is designed for both small-scale and commercial growers.

Tools used

Web app hosted on Vercel, with Leaflet maps and Esri imagery. Hardware: ESP32, soil moisture probe, soil salinity probe, waterproof probe, solar panel and charge module, 18650 battery, programmed in Arduino IDE (C++). Design: Autodesk Fusion for the enclosure, 3D printed in PETG.

Creativity

The name comes from the falaj, the traditional irrigation channels of the UAE and Oman, reflecting our aim to connect local farming heritage with space data. Arabic captions, palm-row intercropping trials and UAE-specific planting windows make the platform designed for this region, not adapted from somewhere else. Pairing satellite data with our own ground sensor lets us check and sharpen coarse satellite readings at farm level.

What we considered

We focused on accessibility for farmers, regional climate variation and data reliability. We are open about current limits. The app uses Umm Al Quwain as a reference site with example inputs, and satellite data such as SMAP is coarse in resolution, which is why we built a ground sensor.
